extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry/drama (playwrights, critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Aristotle's criteria for comedy and distinctions between epic and tragedy: definitions of the Ridiculous, necessary dramatic elements, the role of plot/fable, and differences of form, length, and constituents between epic and tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as imitation of men worse than the average
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comedy ... is an imitation of men worse than the average; worse, however, not as regards any and every sort of fault, but only as regards one particular kind, the Ridiculous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle frames comedy as a representational art that depicts human characters who are inferior to the average in a specific way (the Ridiculous), rather than depicting people who are morally evil or harmful. This sets an evaluative boundary: comedic characters should be comedic via their ridiculousness, not through causing real harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and handling of the Ridiculous
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Ridiculous may be defined as a mistake or deformity not productive of pain or harm to others; the mask, for instance, that excites laughter, is something ugly and distorted without causing pain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ridiculous is explicitly a sub-species of the Ugly and is characterized by harmless error or deformity. Effective comedy aims to provoke laughter through this harmless defect or mistake rather than through cruelty or injury. The mask example illustrates that distortion which does not cause pain is appropriate material for laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent elements of early Comedy (chorus, masks, prologues, multiple actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early comedy featured elements such as a chorus of comedians (initially volunteers, later officially granted by the archon), masks, prologues, and a plurality of actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are structural/practical features historically associated with comedic performance. While Aristotle notes the historic uncertainty about who introduced items like masks and prologues, their presence is treated as characteristic of the genre and relevant when considering form and staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should employ an invented fable/plot rather than invective
rubrics_metrics.description: "The invented Fable, or Plot, however, originated in Sicily ... of Athenian poets Crates was the first to drop the Comedy of invective and frame stories of a general and non-personal nature, in other words, Fables or Plots."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle endorses the use of constructed plots (fables) in comedy that are general and non-personal, as opposed to mere invective or personal attack. A strong comedic work, by this standard, organizes its material into an invented narrative rather than relying on direct abuse or topical insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic as imitation of serious subjects in a grand kind of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: "Epic poetry ... is an imitation of serious subjects in a grand kind of verse. It differs ... in that it is in one kind of verse and in narrative form."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic and tragedy share a seriousness of subject and elevated style, but epic is specifically narrative and composed in a single kind of verse. When evaluating or composing epic poetry, emphasis should be on sustained narrative and consistent verse form rather than dramatic presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope: epic unconstrained; tragedy aims for unity of time
rubrics_metrics.description: "[Epic differs] in its length—which is due to its action having no fixed limit of time, whereas Tragedy endeavours to keep as far as possible within a single circuit of the sun, or something near that."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One formal distinction is the permitted temporal extent of the action: epic narratives may span long or indefinite periods, while tragedy is expected to confine its action roughly to a single day (unity of time). This informs judgments about appropriate scale and pacing for each genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent overlap: epic includes parts of tragedy; tragedy has additional parts
rubrics_metrics.description: "They differ also ... in their constituents, some being common to both and others peculiar to Tragedy ... All the parts of an epic are included in Tragedy; but those of Tragedy are not all of them to be found in the Epic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle asserts that tragedy is in some sense a more complex or comprehensive form: everything found in epic can be present in tragedy, but tragedy contains additional constituent elements. Consequently, someone competent to judge tragedy is also competent to judge epic—implying a hierarchy of evaluative demands between the genres.
